What Is a Chakra? Meaning, Origin & How the System Developed

What does "chakra" actually mean, where does the concept come from, and how did the seven-chakra system as we know it develop over time?

Key Takeaways

  • •The word "chakra" is Sanskrit for "wheel" or "disc," describing a point where subtle energy is said to gather in the body.
  • •Chakras were first described in early Yoga Upanishads and developed more fully in medieval tantric texts.
  • •The now-common seven-chakra model is a later synthesis — some classical texts describe different numbers or arrangements.
  • •The chakra system entered Western wellness culture largely through 20th-century translations and yoga's global spread.
Parikshiva Published July 28, 2026 2 min read

A chakra, in the yogic and tantric traditions of India, is a symbolic point along the body's central axis where subtle life-force — prana — is said to gather and express itself through a particular life theme. The word itself comes from Sanskrit, and understanding its literal meaning is the clearest way into the whole system.

What Does "Chakra" Actually Mean?

Chakra (चक्र) is Sanskrit for "wheel" or "disc." The image is deliberate: each centre is traditionally described as a spinning wheel of energy, rather than a static point. This is why chakras are so often illustrated as circular, lotus-like forms in traditional art — the wheel imagery isn't decorative, it's central to what the word itself is describing.

Where Does the Concept Come From?

The earliest textual references to chakra-like centres appear in the Yoga Upanishads, a group of texts composed roughly between the last centuries BCE and the early centuries CE. The system was developed much further within medieval tantric literature, particularly texts associated with Hatha Yoga and Kaula tantra, which is where the now-familiar seven-centre model, along with seed mantras, lotus-petal counts, and presiding deities for each chakra, was systematised in real detail.

Was the System Always Seven Chakras?

Not exactly. Different tantric schools describe varying numbers and arrangements of chakras — some texts describe five, some describe more than seven, and some include additional minor centres alongside the main ones. The seven-chakra model most people encounter today is a later synthesis that became the dominant teaching framework, especially as it was translated and popularised in the 20th century.

How Chakras Reached Western Wellness Culture

The chakra system entered widespread Western awareness largely through early-20th-century translations of tantric texts, followed by the global spread of yoga as a physical and spiritual practice later in the century. Along the way, some elements — particularly the now-standard color associations — were added or adapted by Western teachers rather than drawn directly from the earliest Sanskrit sources.

A traditional framework, not a scientific one

Chakras are a symbolic system from a long-standing spiritual and philosophical tradition. They have not been anatomically verified by modern science, and understanding their history is a matter of intellectual and cultural interest — not a medical claim.

✦ Good to Know

Frequently Asked

Which ancient texts first describe the chakra system?

The earliest references appear in the Yoga Upanishads, composed roughly between the last centuries BCE and the early centuries CE. The system was developed in much greater detail later, in medieval tantric texts associated with Hatha Yoga.

Is the 7-chakra system the only version described in the tradition?

No. Different tantric schools describe varying numbers and arrangements of energy centres — some with five, some with more than seven, and some including additional minor points. The seven-chakra model is a later synthesis that became the standard teaching framework, but it is not the only historical version.

How did chakras become popular in the West?

Largely through early-20th-century English translations of tantric texts, followed by the global spread of yoga as both a physical and spiritual practice later in the century. Some familiar elements, especially the standard color scheme, were adapted or added by Western teachers along the way rather than drawn directly from the oldest Sanskrit sources.

Is "chakra" a Hindu or Buddhist concept?

Chakra-like subtle-body centres appear in both Hindu tantric traditions and in Vajrayana Buddhist tantra, each with somewhat different names, numbers and interpretations. The seven-chakra model most widely taught today draws primarily from the Hindu tantric and Hatha Yoga lineage.

Did the number of chakras always used to be seven?

No — the number seven became the dominant teaching model over time, but earlier and parallel texts describe different counts and arrangements. The consistency you see today across yoga studios and wellness apps reflects a widely-adopted modern convention more than a single unchanging ancient rule.
